title: NIST Releases Final IR 8547 Establishing Definitive Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition Timeline and Deprecation Schedules - Quantum Computing Report
gist: NIST finalized IR 8547, setting that quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035, with federal high-value assets required to move key establishment by end-2030 and signatures by end-2031, and approving hybrid PQC-plus-classical schemes under FIPS 140.

insights.claim: NIST issued final IR 8547, 'Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards', giving agencies and enterprises the official timeline for phasing out classical public-key cryptography.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The definitive reference that compliance programs will be built around.

insights.claim: Under White House Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, federal High Value Assets must complete PQC transition for key establishment by December 31, 2030 and digital signatures by December 31, 2031.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Binding federal dates set the start of procurement cycles for PQC vendors.

insights.claim: NIST confirms classical quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms will be deprecated after 2030 and completely disallowed after 2035 across the broader IT ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A 2035 hard stop gives a ten-year addressable window for migration spending.

insights.claim: Quantum-vulnerable standards include RSA and DH/ECDH for key establishment and RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA for signatures, with ML-KEM (FIPS 203, default ML-KEM-768), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) as targets, and HQC and FN-DSA still under development.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Defines the algorithms that PQC products must support.
insights.locator: NIST IR 8547: Cryptographic Migration & Deprecation Framework

insights.claim: NIST anchors urgency on Mosca's theorem and Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks, since adversaries siphon encrypted traffic to decrypt once cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers mature.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Confidentiality risk exists today, which justifies spending before CRQCs arrive.
insights.locator: Addressing the Asymmetry of Cryptographic Threat Horizons

insights.claim: Key encapsulation is the immediate priority because intercepted ciphertext cannot be re-encrypted retroactively; NIST mandates federal enforcement of TLS 1.3 by January 2, 2030 and advises deploying hybrid ML-KEM plus classical Diffie-Hellman key exchange immediately.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: TLS and VPN endpoints are first in line for upgrades.

insights.claim: Digital signatures are immune to HNDL collection because authenticity is evaluated at signing time, but replacing PKI certificates, root CAs, PIV smart cards and HSMs creates logistical friction that historically requires decade-long conversion cycles.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Signature migration is a slow, complexity-driven opportunity for PKI and HSM vendors.

insights.claim: NIST updated SP 800-56C and SP 800-227 so a PQC shared secret such as ML-KEM can be concatenated with a classical secret such as ECDH without invalidating FIPS 140 module validation, even if one input is from an unapproved legacy algorithm.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Removes a regulatory obstacle to hybrid deployments.

insights.claim: NIST also accommodates dual signatures combining classical and quantum-resistant algorithms in certificates and software binaries, provided at least one component is NIST-approved.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Allows phased signature migration without waiting for full replacement.
insights.locator: Similarly, NIST guidelines accommodate dual signatures

insights.claim: Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS, HSS, XMSS, XMSSMT) are approved strictly for software, firmware and secure boot signing because of state-tracking operational overhead, and AES, SHA-2/SHA-3 and Ascon remain approved while 112-bit legacy primitives are disallowed after 2030.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Symmetric crypto is not the migration problem; firmware signing has a specific approved path.

insights.claim: IBM launched a unified 'IBM Quantum Safe' suite at IBM TechXchange to automate discovery of cryptographic artifacts, generate Cryptography Bills of Materials (CBOMs) and mediate hybrid traffic across legacy networks.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Large vendors are packaging PQC migration products as the regulatory trigger lands.

insights.claim: As the Cryptographic Module Validation Program accelerates validation queues for native FIPS 203, 204 and 205 implementations, the transition is moving from standard-setting to operational enterprise compliance.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Validated modules will gate which vendors can sell to regulated buyers.
insights.locator: As the Cryptographic Module Validation Program
